strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: recasting multi-turn Text-to-SQL as an MDP with explicit propose→execute→verify→refine cycles distinguishes the work from short-horizon translation approaches.

Comprehensive training pipeline (difficulty-aware self-taught warm-start SFT with reject sampling, curriculum RL with multi-level outcome + process rewards) that is described at a level of detail sufficient to reimplement, with extensive hyperparameters and tool configurations in the appendix.

Broad empirical evaluation on two standard benchmarks (CoSQL, SParC) with in-domain and out-of-domain settings, multiple backbones (1.7B/4B), staged ablations (SFT rounds, outcome-only vs. outcome+process RL), action-level ablations (EXECUTE / MEMORY-VERIFY), and difficulty/turn-wise analyses.

Meaningful analysis beyond headline numbers: evolution of five long-horizon capabilities, error-taxonomy analysis with an LLM-as-judge, latency/token-cost reporting (honest about the ~50x token overhead vs. short-horizon SFT), and case studies illustrating the failure modes addressed.

Baselines span frontier LLMs, prompting agents (CoE-SQL, ACT-SQL), and pre-LLM models, and the main results (e.g., 72.0 average for the 4B model) represent credible state-of-the-art claims at these model sizes.
weaknesses: Potential test-time information leakage in the memory tool: the appendix tool configuration and case studies show the memory retrieves the GROUND-TRUTH SQL of prior turns ('A tool for retrieving the historical questions and ground-truth SQL in this dialogue'). If this oracle access is used at evaluation time, the model has substantially richer context than all baselines, which only see prior questions/utterances. The paper is ambiguous about whether prior-turn SQL in memory is gold or the model's own predictions, and this is never addressed — it could materially inflate the reported gains.

The process rewards are heavily gold-supervised: Clause-Match F1 against the reference SQL for PROPOSE/SELF-CORRECT/M-VERIFY, and EX/EM against gold execution/string. This makes dense RL closer to additional gold-conditioned SFT than genuinely self-directed agentic learning, weakening the claim that the policy 'autonomously learned' long-horizon behavior; the contribution of RL vs. extra exposure to gold supervision is not disentangled.

Reproducibility is not yet demonstrated: code, data, and models are promised 'after the internal review' and are not available at submission time; reward weights are selected by grid search on a 'small held-out subset' whose construction and exact weight values are not reported.

No statistical significance testing or variance estimates for the benchmark comparisons; several gains (e.g., 70.4 vs. 70.2 average for the 4B short-horizon SFT baseline) are small, and prompt sensitivity is not analyzed despite multi-turn agentic prompting being notoriously high-variance.

Comparison fairness concerns beyond memory: baseline numbers are partly taken from prior reports under potentially different prompting/protocols, and the long-horizon evaluation framework (tool calls, 8000-token cap, max 4 interactions) is not applied uniformly to all baselines; six residual failures attributed to the token cap suggest the budget choices matter.

The 'first' claim (first multi-turn Text-to-SQL agent with execution- and memory-based verification/self-correction) is somewhat overstated given prior edit-based/self-correcting multi-turn systems and RL-with-environment-interaction work (Search-R1, WebAgent-R1); positioning should be more careful.

Presentation issues: Figure 2's error-percentage breakdown lacks provenance; duplicate references (Ma et al. 2025a/b are the same arXiv paper); inconsistent naming (COSQL vs. CoSQL, 'Qwen4B' in appendix headers); the reward tables and Equation (1) transition rules are dense and could be clearer.

strengths: Extensive evaluation across four research questions with ablations (warm-start rounds, outcome vs. process rewards, EXECUTE/MEMORY-VERIFY removal, turn-wise and difficulty-wise breakdowns, error taxonomy), which is more thorough than many similar agentic-RL papers

Consistent empirical gains: the proposed method outperforms same-size baselines and several much larger models on CoSQL and SParC in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings, with a fair short-horizon SFT baseline trained on the same data

The pipeline is carefully engineered and documented: detailed hyperparameters, tool configurations, prompts, training dynamics (reward, entropy, response length), and latency/token-cost statistics are provided, supporting reproducibility; the authors also promise full release of code, models, and trajectories

The core idea of explicitly verifying against the database and a dialogue memory during training (rather than treating multi-turn T2SQL as pure translation) is sensible and directly addresses real failure modes (execution errors, cross-turn incoherence) evidenced in Fig. 2 and Fig. 7
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the contribution is largely an assembly of established techniques (STaR-style self-taught reject sampling, GRPO, curriculum RL, tool-interaction RL à la Search-R1/WebAgent-R1) applied to a new task setting; the 'first' claims in the abstract and conclusion overstate the delta over prior multi-turn T2SQL work

A potentially serious evaluation ambiguity: the memory_retrieve tool description (Appendix B.0.1) and trajectory examples (Fig. 3, Appendix D) show the memory containing the ground-truth SQL and parsed elements of previous turns. The paper never clarifies whether, at test time, the memory stores gold or model-generated SQL from prior turns. If gold history is used, the reported gains may be partly an artifact of the evaluation protocol; if model-generated, the protocol is standard but the paper must say so explicitly

A key ablation is missing: a short-horizon RL baseline (GRPO trained directly on final SQL without tools/environment). Without it, it is impossible to isolate whether the gains come from the long-horizon tool loop or simply from RL on the same data

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed variance on the main results; several headline margins (e.g., 1.7B RL vs. short-horizon SFT on EM) are small enough that this matters

The M-VERIFY process reward is defined via clause-F1 against the gold SQL, which invites reward hacking (rewarding superficial clause similarity rather than genuine coherence verification); no analysis of reward hacking or verification-action quality is provided

Cost trade-off is severe and under-discussed: the method uses ~2,400 tokens and 16–28s per query versus ~50 tokens and ~1s for short-horizon SFT (Table 8), a 30–50x latency increase that receives only a single sentence
The error analysis relies on GPT-5 as judge with no human validation of the taxonomy classifications, weakening the RQ3 conclusions (e.g., about Aggregation Drift)

Presentation issues: duplicated SQL-R1 citations (2025a/2025b), inconsistent narrative around Table 2 markers (e.g., Finding 2 discusses 14B behavior that is only partially visible in the table), and the MDP 'violation set' computed at M-VERIFY is never specified

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: identifying lack of execution-based verification and self-correction in multi-turn Text-to-SQL, and casting the task as an MDP with a propose-execute-verify-refine loop is a sensible and clearly articulated formulation.

Strong and consistent empirical gains: the method improves over matched-size short-horizon SFT baselines (e.g., 4B: 72.0 -> 72.0 average but with larger EX and out-of-domain gains; 1.7B: 65.9 -> 69.5) and outperforms prompting-based agents (CoE-SQL, ACT-SQL) and several much larger frontier models on CoSQL/SParC.

Comprehensive evaluation structure around four research questions, with ablations covering training stages, the necessity of both EXECUTE and MEMORY-VERIFY actions, outcome vs. process rewards, turn-wise and difficulty-wise analyses, and training dynamics (reward, entropy, response length).

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: detailed implementation appendix (LlamaFactory/DeepSpeed, Verl/GRPO config, tool schemas, prompts, LLM-as-judge prompt, full hyperparameters), and a commitment to releasing code, models, logs, and trajectories.

Useful analysis of long-horizon capability evolution (function calling, verification, self-correction) and error-taxonomy analysis showing which failure modes are reduced (execution errors, constraint coherence, join path) versus persistent ones (aggregation drift on extra-hard queries), which is honest and informative.
weaknesses: Potential information-leakage concerns in the setup: the memory-retrieval tool is described as retrieving 'historical questions and ground-truth SQL' from previous turns, and both the SFT trajectories and the M-VERIFY/PROPOSE process rewards rely on gold SQL clause-level F1. The paper does not clearly establish whether, at test time, memory contains gold SQL for prior turns or the model's own predictions; if gold SQL is used, the evaluation setting is optimistic and the 'autonomous' verification claim is overstated. This needs explicit clarification.

Novelty is mostly in combination rather than in technique: warm-start SFT via reject sampling (STaR/RFT-style), GRPO with loss masking, curriculum RL, and execution-feedback self-correction are all established components. The paper's contribution claims (e.g., 'the first multi-turn Text-to-SQL agent with explicit verification') should be more carefully scoped, and the MDP formalism is largely descriptive since the action-transition rule is deterministic and heavily scripted.

Baseline comparability is not fully convincing: previous reported results for GPT-4.1/O3/RASAT+PICARD were presumably obtained under different prompts/protocols; the paper does not report running frontier baselines under the same harness. Claims of state-of-the-art 'across various model sizes' rest on training only 1.7B and 4B backbones.

No statistical significance testing or multiple-seed variance is reported; several key comparisons (e.g., 4B short-horizon SFT 70.4 vs. ours 72.0 average) are within a couple of points, so significance is unclear.
Error analysis uses an LLM-as-judge (GPT-5) taxonomy without human validation or inter-annotator agreement, weakening RQ3 conclusions.

Cost/efficiency is a real trade-off: ~28s latency and ~2400 tokens per query versus ~1s/50 tokens for short-horizon SFT; while acknowledged, the practical deployability framing could be more balanced, and a cost-matched comparison is absent.

The reward-weight grid search is described only briefly ('selected via grid search on a small held-out subset'), and the curriculum itself is never ablated (all RL runs use it), so attributions among curriculum, process reward, and outcome reward are incomplete.

Presentation issues: duplicated SQL-R1 references (2025a/b are the same paper), the odd 'K Team' citation for Kimi K1.5, several grammatical errors (e.g., Figure 2 caption), and some inconsistencies between stated rollout counts (20 in Algorithm 1/curriculum vs. n=5 in the config appendix) that hinder exact reproduction.

strengths: The paper presents a complete, well-motivated agentic training pipeline (self-taught warm-start SFT with difficulty-aware rejection sampling, followed by curriculum GRPO with multi-level outcome + process rewards) for multi-turn Text-to-SQL, a setting that prior RL-based reasoning work has largely ignored.

The empirical study is unusually thorough: in-domain and out-of-domain results on CoSQL/SparC, two model scales (1.7B/4B) plus a third backbone (LLaMA-3.2-3B), ablations of EX/EM rewards, ablations removing EXECUTE and MEMORY-VERIFY actions, turn-wise and difficulty-wise analyses, token/latency Pareto analysis, error-taxonomy analysis with an LLM-as-judge, and training dynamics — collectively providing strong evidence that the reported gains (+4–5 EX over the best short-horizon RL baseline) come from the proposed long-horizon design rather than incidental factors.

Reproducibility is well supported: the appendix includes the full self-taught SFT algorithm, tool schemas, reward tables, complete hyperparameters, and case studies; the authors commit to releasing full recipes.
The MDP formulation and action/transition specification (Eq. 1) are clearly written, and the loss-masking and reward design are precisely defined, making the method easy to reimplement.
The robustness experiment conditioning on model-generated (rather than gold) dialogue history (Table 6) is a valuable and honest addition that many multi-turn parsing papers omit.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is incremental: the pipeline is a competent composition of known components (STaR-style rejection sampling, GRPO with token-level advantages, process rewards, tool-use agents). The 'first multi-turn' claim in Table 1 is somewhat overstated, since the delta over existing agent frameworks (CoE-SQL, ACT-SQL) is primarily training-based rather than a fundamentally new capability.

The MEMORY-VERIFY process reward is computed against the gold SQL (AVG F1 over clauses, 1−F1 on failure). This means 'coherence verification' during training is largely gold-supervised rather than learned from genuinely unsupervised coherence signals, which weakens the central claim that the agent learns environment- and memory-driven verification; a coherence reward that does not require gold labels would substantially strengthen the contribution.

Statistical rigor is limited: most main results lack variance estimates or significance testing (std is reported only for the reward ablation in Table 10), and no number of runs is stated; given single-run RL training, some gains (e.g., +0.2 to +1 EM margins) could be within noise.

The default evaluation protocol populates dialogue history with ground-truth SQL; while the authors do provide a predicted-prior variant, the headline numbers in Table 2 are for the more favorable setting.

Practicality concerns: the method incurs substantial latency (~28s) and token cost, and its advantage over the short-horizon SFT baseline (73.1 EX at 1s/49 tokens) trades a large efficiency gap for accuracy — the paper discusses this honestly but it limits immediate applicability.
The memory module is a prompt-engineered text store with a fixed checklist verifier; scalability to industrial schemas is only discussed speculatively (future work) rather than evaluated.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation on two standard multi-turn Text-to-SQL benchmarks (CoSQL, SParC) with multiple model scales (Qwen3-1.7B/4B, LLaMA3.2-3B), covering ablations on reward components (Table 10), removal of EXECUTE/M-VERIFY actions (Table 3), turn-wise and difficulty-wise breakdowns, and out-of-domain generalization.

The robustness experiment conditioning on model-generated prior SQL (Table 6) addresses a known weakness of the standard gold-history evaluation protocol and is a genuine addition over prior multi-turn work.

Detailed implementation documentation: full hyperparameters, tool configurations, prompts, and the self-taught SFT algorithm are provided in the appendix, supporting reproducibility if code is released as promised.
The training pipeline (difficulty-aware rejection sampling, curriculum RL, process rewards) is clearly described and the stages are individually ablated, so the source of gains can be traced.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the framework is a combination of well-established techniques (STaR-style rejection-sampling SFT, GRPO, tool-integrated RL as in Search-R1/WebAgent-R1, partial/reward shaping as in Reasoning-SQL) applied to multi-turn Text-to-SQL. The 'first multi-turn Text-to-SQL framework with verification and self-correction' claim is overstated; CoE-SQL and edit-based approaches already perform iterative refinement, just not via RL.

The MDP formulation is largely decorative. Equation (1) prescribes a deterministic action sequence (PROPOSE→EXECUTE→E-VERIFY→M-VERIFY→FINALIZE), so the 'autonomously learned policy' is effectively a scripted tool loop; the framing inflates the apparent contribution.

Process rewards are computed against the gold SQL (clause-level F1 for PROPOSE/SELF-CORRECT and M-VERIFY), which conflates learned verification with dense gold supervision and risks reward hacking toward gold-SQL text rather than genuine self-verification. The E-VERIFY reward table (e.g., 0.1 for null results) appears arbitrary and is not justified.

Gains over the strongest matched baseline are moderate (~3-4 EX points) and reported without statistical significance testing (standard deviations appear only for one ablation table), making it hard to judge robustness of the improvement.

Default evaluation uses ground-truth SQL for dialogue history, which overstates real-world multi-turn performance; the more realistic predicted-prior evaluation is only run on CoSQL with one baseline pair.
The error analysis (Fig. 6) relies on GPT-5 as an LLM-as-judge with a novel taxonomy designed by the authors; no human validation of the judge's classifications is reported.
Reward weights are selected by grid search on held-out training data, and no code or data is released at submission time ('upon acceptance'), which currently limits reproducibility.

Writing and presentation issues: the Results sections read as a repetitive list of bolded 'Result 1..12' claims; baseline rows mix closed-source prompting results with fine-tuned model comparisons in ways that complicate interpretation; several tables (e.g., Table 2) are dense and hard to parse.
Only older benchmarks (CoSQL/SParC, 2019) are used for the core claims; BIRD/Spider evaluation is a small proof-of-concept without the agentic training on those datasets.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: recasting multi-turn Text-to-SQL as a long-horizon MDP with explicit environment verification (EXECUTE) and memory-based coherence verification is a natural but non-trivial extension of prior single-turn RL work (SQL-R1, Reasoning-SQL), and Table 1 positions the contribution carefully against prior systems.

The three-stage pipeline (MDP formulation -> self-taught warm-start SFT with difficulty-aware rejection sampling -> GRPO with multi-level outcome+process rewards) is described in enough algorithmic and hyperparameter detail (Appendices A-C, including tool configs and full verl configs) to make reproduction plausible.

Comprehensive empirical support: gains on both CoSQL and Spider (in-domain and out-of-domain), across two backbone scales (1.7B/4B) and a third base model (LLaMA-3.2-3B), with ablations on each action type (Table 3), each reward component (Table 10), reward-only vs outcome-only training, turn-wise and difficulty-wise breakdowns, training dynamics, and efficiency/latency trade-offs.

The analysis goes beyond headline numbers: error taxonomy with LLM-as-judge (Fig. 6), Pareto frontier analysis of latency vs accuracy (Table 13), and the 'Predicted as Prior' robustness evaluation (Table 6) that honestly tests deployment conditions where ground-truth history is unavailable.
The self-taught warm-start procedure (coverage statistics in Table 9) is a reasonable and well-motivated answer to the known problem that naive SFT on gold answers produces unnatural trajectories.
weaknesses: Some process-reward components are gold-dependent in ways that risk teaching the model to game the reward rather than verify correctly: the M-VERIFY reward uses AVG-F1 against the gold SQL's parsed clauses, so the model is rewarded for producing verification verdicts that align with gold-consistency, which may not transfer to genuinely unseen error types; the intuition is stated but the risk of reward hacking is not analyzed.

Fairness of the central 'short-horizon vs long-horizon' comparison is not fully controlled: the short-horizon RL baselines are re-implementations, and it is unclear whether they received equivalent tuning effort, rollout budgets, and max-token allowances; the latency comparisons in Table 13 involve different token budgets by construction, making the Pareto claims partially built-in.

The efficiency story is mixed and the paper leans on a citation about latency tolerance; the method roughly triples token generation and latency relative to short-horizon SFT, and the claim of 'Pareto frontier' is asserted from the authors' own measurement setup (unoptimized vLLM), which is acknowledged but softens the practical significance claim.

Statistical rigor is limited: several results are single-run numbers without variance or significance testing (the reward ablation reports ±std but the main Table 2 does not); the LLM-as-judge error analysis uses GPT-5 without reported judge agreement/validation against human labels.

Reproducibility is promised ('full recipes will be released upon acceptance') rather than demonstrated; no code or data link is currently available, and some details (e.g., grid-searched reward weights on a 'small held-out validation subset') are underspecified, raising mild overfitting concerns for the final reward configuration.

Novelty is incremental at the component level: each ingredient (GRPO, tool-interaction RL, rejection-sampling SFT, process rewards) is established; the contribution is primarily their composition and adaptation to multi-turn Text-to-SQL, which limits prospective impact beyond this task.
